entry.title: NANLITE Rapid Square, Rectangular and Octagonal Softboxes Announced – Bowens Mount, Eggcrate Included, Plus a 10cm NANLUX Diffusion Ball
entry.summary: NANLITE has added three umbrella-style softboxes to its Rapid line: the Rapid 90 Square, the Rapid 100×70 Rectangular and the Rapid 120 Octagonal. All three fit Bowens and BE mount fixtures, have a silver interior, and come with two diffusers, an eggcrate grid and a carrying bag,
entry.content:
NANLITE has added three umbrella-style softboxes to its Rapid line: the Rapid 90 Square, the Rapid 100×70 Rectangular and the Rapid 120 Octagonal. All three fit Bowens and BE mount fixtures, have a silver interior, and come with two diffusers, an eggcrate grid and a carrying bag, at US prices from $89 to $109. Sister brand NANLUX has also released a 10cm FE mount diffusion ball for the Evoke 150C. Here are the details.

We reported on the NANLITE Rapid 90 and Rapid 120 parabolic softboxes in January 2025. Those are deep 16-rib parabolic modifiers with a flat-folding design, and they launched at $179 and $199 (NANLITE’s US store now lists them at $129 and $149). The three new models are a simpler and less expensive option. They use an umbrella-style frame with aluminum alloy rods (four in the square and rectangular versions, eight in the octagonal one) and nylon fabric. NANLITE positions them for portraits, interviews and other soft key light work, in the studio and on location.

Three shapes, one kit

The Rapid 90 Square (SB-S-RP90) measures 90 x 90cm / 35.4 x 35.4in. The Rapid 100×70 Rectangular (SB-RT-RP100×70) measures 100 x 70cm / 39.4 x 27.6in with a depth of 32cm / 12.6in. The Rapid 120 Octagonal (SB-O-RP120) has a diameter of 120cm / 47.2in and a depth of 36cm / 14.2in.

Each softbox comes with an interior and an exterior diffuser. With both diffusers in place, NANLITE specifies a beam angle of 110°. The included eggcrate narrows this to 70° on the Rapid 90 Square and to 60° on the rectangular and octagonal models. The diffusers and the grid can also be used separately.

Folded, the softboxes are between 875mm / 34.4in (rectangular) and 912mm / 35.9in (square) long, and all three use the same 360 x 1095mm / 14.2 x 43.1in carrying bag. The softbox alone weighs 0.82kg / 1.81lb for the square model, 0.85kg / 1.87lb for the rectangular one and 1.08kg / 2.38lb for the octagonal one. The eggcrate adds 0.12 to 0.17kg / 0.27 to 0.38lb, and the bag weighs 0.37kg / 0.82lb.

Which lights fit?

All three softboxes have a Bowens mount and also fit fixtures with BE mount, which is the NANLUX version of the Bowens mount with electronic contacts. NANLITE lists the FC-300B, FC-500B and FC-500C, the FC-720B and FC-720C, the FS-150, FS-200 and FS-300 families including the FS-300C, and the Forza 200, 300, 300B, 500, 500B II, 720 and 720B. On the NANLUX side, the list includes the Evoke 600C. Other Bowens mount lights should fit as well, but NANLITE’s compatibility list only names its own fixtures.

NANLUX FE mount diffusion ball 10cm

NANLUX has also released the MD-DB-FE10, a 10cm diffusion ball with FE mount. It fits FE and FM mount fixtures, including the Evoke 150C. It is a smaller version of the 15cm FE and 20cm BE diffusion balls that NANLUX released in October 2025. The ball measures 96 x 92.2mm / 3.78 x 3.63in and weighs 0.03kg / 0.07lb.

According to NANLUX, the ball spreads the fixture’s focused beam into a wide, soft source with hemispherical coverage. The spec sheet gives a beam angle of 110°. Unlike the two larger balls, which NANLUX rates IP66, the 10cm version has no IP rating in its specifications. For Evoke 150C users who already carry the FE30 parallel beam reflector or the FL-12 Fresnel, it adds a soft-light option that weighs almost nothing.

Price and availability

In the US, the softboxes are available for pre-order from NANLITE: the Rapid 100×70 Rectangular costs $89, the Rapid 90 Square costs $99 and the Rapid 120 Octagonal costs $109. NANLITE gives a 2-year warranty. The NANLUX 10cm diffusion ball costs $17.90. At the time of writing, B&H and CVP do not list the new products, and we have not seen European prices yet.

Do you use umbrella-style softboxes on your Bowens mount lights, or do you prefer deeper parabolic modifiers? Which of the three shapes would you choose for interviews? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Strada for Apple Vision Pro Released – Stream Apple Immersive Video From Any Mac, Immersive Dailies From BRAW
entry.summary: Strada now runs on Apple Vision Pro. The cloud-free collaboration platform streams Apple Immersive Video straight from a remote Mac into the headset, lets reviewers leave time-stamped comments without taking the headset off, and can turn camera-original Blackmagic RAW into immers
entry.content:
Strada now runs on Apple Vision Pro. The cloud-free collaboration platform streams Apple Immersive Video straight from a remote Mac into the headset, lets reviewers leave time-stamped comments without taking the headset off, and can turn camera-original Blackmagic RAW into immersive dailies on the machine where the footage sits. No upload, no HLS packaging, no cloud bucket.

I have been following Strada closely since Strada Agents at NAB 2025, and the company has moved fast this year: Strada Connect at NAB 2026, our Strada 2 first look at Cine Gear, and the Strada 2.0 release in August. The idea behind all of it is the same: your media stays on your own drive, and collaborators reach it over a peer-to-peer connection. Strada published a new demo video today, “Strada Meets Apple Vision Pro”, and it takes that idea into a place where it makes even more sense than on the desktop.

Why immersive video needs this

Anyone who has worked on an Apple Immersive project knows the problem. The format is captured at 90 frames per second and more than 50MP per eye, as we explained in our report on the Apple Immersive Video updates at WWDC26. Files of that size are slow to upload, and getting a cut in front of a director or a client who sits in another city usually means export, packaging, hosting, and waiting. Productions such as the Red Bull big wave surfing film or the Cirrus immersive film show how many people now shoot for the headset, and review is still one of the weak links.

Strada’s answer is to skip the hosting step completely. On its Vision Pro page, the company puts it simply: “No HLS playlists. No cloud uploads.” You share a single file or a whole folder of AIVU files, the format Apple uses for Apple Immersive Video, and your collaborator opens it in Strada on Vision Pro and streams it from your Mac over the internet. According to Strada, there is “nothing to upload, package or host.”

Browse, play, comment

The demo video is built around three steps, which Strada calls “Browse → Play → Comment”. Inside the headset, you see every drive that is connected through Strada, move through the project folders, and open a clip. In the screenshots Strada provides, two Macs (one in Colorado, one in Los Angeles) show up under “My Devices”, and a folder of AIVU clips between 1.2 and 4.7GB each sits ready to play.

The part that interests me most is review. A reviewer watches the immersive clip and adds comments without leaving the shot, and every note lands on the exact frame with its timecode. Strada says you can choose who sees each comment, and the screenshots show a visibility menu set to “Everyone” next to a text field. According to Strada, the notes go right back to the team, so nobody has to type up notes from a phone call afterwards.

Immersive dailies straight from Blackmagic RAW

For productions, this is the bigger feature. According to Strada, you can point it at a folder of camera-original Blackmagic RAW files on a remote Mac, and it generates the AIVU files right there, on that machine. The company says a remote crew’s dailies can then be watched in Vision Pro “almost instantly, anywhere in the world.” Blackmagic built the URSA Cine Immersive together with Apple for this format, so BRAW is the natural place to start.

This is consistent with what Michael Cioni showed Johnnie at NAB, where Strada played a 28GB BRAW file in a web browser, debayered on the fly, over half a megabit of show-floor internet. Strada’s desktop app already has an “Optimize” function that, according to the company, makes RAW files up to 100 times smaller for editing, and then relinks to the originals for the export. In one of Strada’s screenshots, a “BRAW DAILIES” folder of 128.61GB becomes about 179.4MB of optimized media. How the AIVU generation works in detail, Strada does not say. My guess is that it uses the same background processing on the host Mac, but that is just my guess.

What we don’t know yet

A few questions are open. Strada’s site describes adaptive playback quality for the desktop app, which steps down when the connection dips and back up when it recovers. The Vision Pro page does not say how the immersive stream behaves on a weak connection, or at what quality a reviewer actually sees the AIVU file. For colorists and directors who judge an immersive shot in the headset, that matters a lot (Michael, if you are reading this: please show the current stream quality inside the player, so a reviewer knows what they are judging).

The other open point is the host. Strada’s Vision Pro page names the Mac as the source in every example, while the desktop app also runs on Windows 11. A Mac with the media must stay online for the stream to work, which is the nature of a peer-to-peer system and the trade-off for not paying for cloud storage.

Price and availability

Strada says the Vision Pro app is available now on the App Store. Strada’s pricing has not changed with this release: the free tier includes viewing of unlimited assets, commenting, and connections to mobile devices, Basic costs $8 per user per month and adds remote editing and unlimited transfers, and Pro costs $24 per user per month. Strada does not say which tier the immersive dailies function requires.

Are you working on Apple Immersive projects, and how do you get immersive dailies in front of your team today? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: RED KOMODO-X Now $2,000 Off at B&H and CVP – Still Worth It?

entry.content:
Black Friday is around the corner, and holiday sales are ramping up. B&H and CVP are currently running a massive holiday sale on RED’s entry-level cinema camera, the KOMODO-X. The offer applies to the body-only option, in either Nikon Z or Canon RF mount, and allows you to get your hands on your first RED camera or pick up a B Cam for just $4,995 (excl. applicable VAT).

Before reading on, please note: offers may be temporary and might end without notice, so make sure to take advantage of this deal before it’s gone. This article reports prices at the time of publication.

When it was first launched in May 2023 for $9,995, the RED KOMODO-X represented a huge upgrade over the original KOMODO, boasting higher frame rates of up to 80fps in 6K .R3D RAW, a locking Canon RF lens mount, an integrated V-mount battery plate, a slightly redesigned body with improved I/O, and much more.

Then, following Nikon’s acquisition of RED, its price was slashed to the current official retail price of $6,995, and a Nikon Z mount version was also introduced. Now, you can get your hands on this 3.5-year-old camera for half of its introductory price. But is it still worth it? Let’s take a closer look!

Is the RED KOMODO-X still worth it in 2026?

As a RED KOMODO-X owner myself, I sometimes wonder whether this camera is still worth investing in as we approach the end of 2026. Of course, the answer is personal and ultimately comes down to the kind of work you do, but I’ll try to give a structured overview of the pros and cons after a year and a half of putting the camera to good use.

I picked up my KOMODO-X last year, as soon as the Nikon Z mount version came out. Undoubtedly, if I were to buy it new today, I would definitely opt for the Nikon Z mount version, unless I were heavily invested in Canon RF glass. Hands down, Nikon’s mirrorless mount is the most adaptable on the market and, following the acquisition, is the most logical choice if you expect support in the long run, or even if you’re planning on pairing the KOMODO-X with a Nikon ZR as a B Cam.

Beyond the lens mount, the biggest selling point for me, as an action-sport filmmaker, was global shutter. Also, as our Lab Test confirmed, despite the global shutter design, the KOMODO-X’s 6K Super35 mm sensor performs very well in terms of dynamic range. The image quality is, indeed, superb and, unless you really need more resolution or higher frame rates, the camera can perform for years to come.

The box-style body also offers professional connectivity such as SDI, XLR audio, and support for functions such as Timecode, Genlock, and remote trigger, making this tiny camera ready for productions of all sizes. Although I might have used some of these connectors only a handful of times, it’s reassuring to know that – with a small investment in a few cables – this I/O is always there if I need it.

Downsides of the RED KOMODO-X

However, all that glitters is not gold. So, on top of the camera body, you have to factor in the cost of accessories and, particularly, CFexpress cards and a good storage solution – both of which are notoriously expensive nowadays. REDCODE RAW .R3D files, paired with RED’s gorgeous exposure tools, are a pleasure to work with, but take up an enormous amount of space, and ProRes only offers marginal gains in this regard.

Although these formats are a perfect fit for most of my productions, I sometimes wish RED would drop a firmware update to add support for Log3G10 recording in a lighter H.265 codec – just like Nikon is about to do with the upcoming Nikon ZR Firmware 2.00 update.

Also, despite firmware 2.2.4 cutting boot-up time by roughly 10 seconds, be ready to wait about 20 seconds for the camera to start up and pack enough V-mount batteries to get you through a full day of shooting, especially if you’re planning on rigging the camera with a high-brightness monitor, a follow focus motor, and a wireless video transmitter.

In short, if you mostly work on run-and-gun projects, I’d honestly discourage you from buying a KOMODO-X, as the workflow and file sizes are likely to quickly turn into a bottleneck. However, if you’re taking cinematography seriously, often work with a crew, and would like a versatile camera for small to mid-sized productions, then I think the KOMODO-X is still worth considering and can serve you well for the foreseeable future.

Price and availability

The RED KOMODO-X is now available for just $4,995 at B&H and €4,540 (excl. VAT) at CVP, which represents a $2,000 discount compared with the official retail price. The offer applies to both the Nikon Z and Canon RF versions of the camera.

For more information, please visit RED’s website here.

Have you been on the fence about whether to buy your first RED camera? Do you think the KOMODO-X is still worth buying as we approach the end of 2026? Let us know your thoughts in the comment section below!

entry.title: RØDE Capture Now Available for Android – Direct Connect for Wireless Micro, Wireless GO (Gen 3) and Wireless PRO, NDI Output
entry.summary: RØDE Capture is now available for Android. The free app brings RØDE’s in-app microphone control to Android phones, together with Direct Connect, which pairs Wireless Micro, Wireless GO (Gen 3) and Wireless PRO transmitters with the phone without a receiver. The Android version al
entry.content:
RØDE Capture is now available for Android. The free app brings RØDE’s in-app microphone control to Android phones, together with Direct Connect, which pairs Wireless Micro, Wireless GO (Gen 3) and Wireless PRO transmitters with the phone without a receiver. The Android version also adds NDI output, so a phone can feed a RØDECaster Video console as an extra camera.

RØDE announced the Android release yesterday. Until now, RØDE Capture was available only for iPhone, where it requires iOS 16 or later. The app combines a video recorder with the settings of the connected RØDE microphone, so users do not need to switch between a camera app and a separate microphone app. RØDE names social media, vlogging, podcasting, mobile journalism and filmmaking as the main uses.

Direct Connect without a receiver

The main feature for Android users is Direct Connect. With it, the transmitters of the Wireless Micro, Wireless GO (Gen 3) and Wireless PRO connect to the phone over Bluetooth, and the receiver stays in the bag. RØDE introduced Direct Connect on iPhone for the Wireless Micro in 2025, as we reported at the time. In February 2026, the company extended it to the Wireless GO (Gen 3) and the Wireless PRO.

For that iPhone rollout, the transmitters needed the latest firmware, which users must install with the desktop version of RØDE Central on a Mac or PC. On iPhone, Direct Connect gives control of the output gain of each transmitter, Split or Merged recording, and the LED brightness. In Merged mode, both transmitters go to both channels of the video file. In Split mode, each transmitter records to its own channel, which gives more control in the edit.

Microphone controls in the app

The available audio controls depend on the connected microphone. According to RØDE, they include gain adjustment, Gain Assist, Noise Reduction, Split or Merged recording and a high-pass filter. The app supports microphones from the RØDE Wireless range, compact on-camera microphones and USB desktop microphones. On iPhone, the list of compatible models includes the Wireless Micro, Wireless GO (Gen 3), Wireless PRO, Wireless ME, Wireless GO II, VideoMic GO II, VideoMic NTG, AI-Micro, NT-USB+ and PodMic USB. RØDE has not published a separate list for Android.

On the video side, users can set the aspect ratio, resolution and frame rate. There are also automatic flash settings and a countdown timer for hands-free recording. On iPhone, the app records in HD, FHD or 4K at 24, 30 or 60fps.

NDI output to RØDECaster Video

The Android release also adds NDI. With it, a phone that runs RØDE Capture becomes an additional video source for the RØDECaster Video, the RØDECaster Video S and the RØDECaster Video Core. NDI inputs came to the consoles with a free firmware update in 2025, and firmware 1.4 added a 4K Capture Mode this September. For a small studio or a live stream, an Android phone can now be a wireless camera angle, as an iPhone already could.

Current limitations

The Android announcement does not list the dual camera modes (split screen and picture-in-picture) that the iPhone version offers. It also does not say whether Dual Cam streaming over NDI, which the iPhone version supports, is available on Android. RØDE has not published a minimum Android version or a list of tested phones. On the day of writing, the description in the Google Play listing still described the iPhone version. Before you use the app on a paid job, test it with your own phone and microphone.

Price and availability

RØDE Capture for Android is available now as a free download from Google Play. The iPhone version is free on the App Store. The three systems that support Direct Connect are the Wireless Micro at $99 or £89, the Wireless GO (Gen 3) at $199 or €152.01 / £154.80, and the Wireless PRO at $274 (regular price $299) or €234.26 / £239.

Do you record audio directly to your phone, or do you still use a receiver? And would you use an Android phone as an NDI camera in your live setup? Let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Adobe Premiere 27.0 Released – Color Mode, AI Assistant Panel, and Generative Audio Tools
entry.summary: Adobe has released Premiere 27.0 with Color Mode, an AI Assistant panel, and tools that generate music, sound effects, and soundscapes in the timeline. The update also retires the Lumetri Color panel, ends support for Intel Macs, and makes the AI Assistant draw Firefly credits wi
entry.content:
Adobe has released Premiere 27.0 with Color Mode, an AI Assistant panel, and tools that generate music, sound effects, and soundscapes in the timeline. The update also retires the Lumetri Color panel, ends support for Intel Macs, and makes the AI Assistant draw Firefly credits with no cost estimate before a prompt runs.

The release arrives during Adobe MAX in Miami Beach. Adobe lists the changes in the Premiere 27.0 release post. Several of the features were in public beta since spring, and we covered the Color Mode beta when Adobe first showed it.

Color Mode replaces the Lumetri Color panel

Color Mode is a dedicated grading workspace behind a new Color tab next to Edit. Adobe describes it as “a dedicated color-grading workspace designed to help you correct individual shots, create consistent looks, and manage color across an entire sequence.” It has a Clip Grid, three operation types (Adjust, Style, and LUT), and grades that apply to a clip, a group, or the complete sequence. A new HSL Masking tool isolates areas by hue, saturation, and luminance and combines with other masks.

The larger change is what goes away. In the Color Mode post, Adobe writes that “the Lumetri Color panel is being retired in Premiere 27.0,” while the Lumetri Color effect stays available and existing grades remain adjustable in Effect Controls. Adobe recommends that editors who are finishing a Lumetri-heavy project complete it in Premiere 26.x first. The company also notes that 8K media can have performance problems in an 8K sequence.

The first user replies under that post are about speed for small jobs. One editor objects that a fast exposure or white balance correction now needs the Color tab or a Lumetri effect on each clip, and another reports that the controls are too sensitive with a pen tablet.

The AI Assistant now uses Firefly credits

The AI Assistant panel reads the project and does editing tasks from plain-language requests. During the beta that started in June, Adobe gave users free daily credits for it. That has ended. In a separate post, community manager Matt Christensen writes that Adobe is “removing the daily and weekly limits on usage” and that “the Assistant will use Firefly credits from your Adobe account’s plan.”

Each response shows the credits it used after the fact. When a user asked if the cost is visible before a request runs, Matt answered: “No, it’s not possible to estimate the amount of credits that will be used when working with the Assistant.” He added that the number depends on the sequence and on the tools the Assistant needs.

Adobe’s own example in that post gives a sense of scale. A request to cut an interview down to the first answer to each question shortened a sequence from 4:43 to about 1:56 and used 19.83 credits. According to Adobe’s generative credits FAQ, Creative Cloud Pro includes 4,000 monthly credits, while Creative Cloud Standard and single-app plans bought since June 17, 2025 include 25. On those plans, this one request is about four fifths of the monthly allowance, and credits do not roll over.

Blackmagic Design took a different route in DaVinci Resolve 21.1, which connects to external AI assistants through MCP and leaves the choice and the cost of the model to the user.

Generative media and audio in the timeline

The Generative Media Tool now creates images, music, and soundscapes in addition to video and sound effects. The editor selects a region in the timeline, types a prompt, and the result goes into the sequence. Generate Music makes instrumental tracks only. Generate Soundscape analyzes the picture and builds ambience and effect layers as a starting point. Generative Extend can now create the missing frames when a clip is too short for a transition.

Unlike the Assistant, these tools show an estimated credit cost before they run. Adobe states that prompts, media, and reference frames “aren’t used to train Adobe or partner AI models.” For partner models, the user is responsible for deciding if the output is appropriate for a project, and some partner models are not available on business plans. The 27.0 posts do not name the partner models. For the previous version, Adobe listed Google Veo, Kling, Runway, and Luma.

Audio, effects, and timeline changes

Separate Crosstalk splits overlapping speakers into separate stems. Auto Ducking now updates its keyframes when clips are added, trimmed, or muted. The Speed/Duration dialog has new audio stretching modes and pitch controls, so a retimed clip does not need a trip to Audition. iXML metadata shows on audio clips in the timeline and Source Monitor, and waveforms draw in real time during recording.

The Effects panel has animated thumbnails and a Preview from Source function. Effects and masks appear as collapsible cards in the Properties panel, Object Mask tracks better, and there are eight new effects, among them Radial Blur and Zoom Blur.

New system requirements

Premiere 27.0 needs Windows 11 version 24H2 or later, or an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later. Intel Macs stay on version 26.x. On Windows, Premiere does not start without a supported GPU. Adobe has also said that version 28.0 will not install on any Windows 10 system. The release adds native Windows on ARM support for systems with the NVIDIA RTX Spark chip, which we reported on in June.

Price and availability

Premiere 27.0 is available now in the Creative Cloud desktop app for current subscribers. Adobe lists Premiere as a single app at $22.99 per month and Creative Cloud Pro at $69.99 per month in the US, both on an annual plan with monthly billing. Additional credit packs start at $9.99 per month for 2,000 credits. For comparison, Blackmagic Design recently cut the one-time price of DaVinci Resolve Studio, and Apple updated Final Cut Pro through Apple Creator Studio (which offers a much more affordable subscription at $12.99 per month for the entire suite, and can still be purchased at a one-time price as well). For more information about the Premiere 27.0 update, please visit the Adobe website.

Do you grade in Premiere, and does a metered AI Assistant change how you plan to use it? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Creator Royalties Hit Record €15.5 Billion, Audiovisual Passes €750 Million – CISAC Global Collections Report 2026
entry.summary: CISAC’s Global Collections Report 2026 is out, and the headline is a record: creators worldwide collected €15.5 billion in royalties in 2025. For filmmakers, the more interesting number is further down in the report. Collections for screenwriters and directors passed €750 million
entry.content:
CISAC’s Global Collections Report 2026 is out, and the headline is a record: creators worldwide collected €15.5 billion in royalties in 2025. For filmmakers, the more interesting number is further down in the report. Collections for screenwriters and directors passed €750 million for the first time, and their income from streaming grew by almost a third. I went through the report to see what it means for people who make films and series, and how much of it is really about AI.

CISAC, the International Confederation of Societies of Authors and Composers, is the umbrella organization for 228 authors’ societies in 111 countries and territories. These societies are collective management organizations: they license the use of creative works and pay the royalties to the authors. One example that many of our readers in Europe know is SACD, which represents screenwriters and directors in France. The 2026 report, which CISAC published on November 4 in its 100th year, covers the 2025 collections for music, audiovisual, visual arts, literature and drama.

The 11.3% headline growth needs a footnote, and CISAC gives it in the report. For the first time, the total includes The Mechanical Licensing Collective (The MLC), the US organization that collects mechanical royalties for songwriters from streaming and download services. The MLC accounts for approximately 52% of the annual increase. Without it, global collections grew by 5.3%, after 6.4% in 2024. That is still growth, but it is a slower pace than the record number suggests.

TV and radio drop to third place

Digital collections rose by 27.9% to €6.57 billion, which is 42.4% of all royalties collected worldwide. In 2016, digital was only €1 billion. Live & Background, the category for concerts and festivals plus music played in shops, restaurants, hotels and gyms, grew to €3.87 billion. With that, it overtook TV & Radio, which fell by 2.6% to €3.82 billion. As recently as 2021, TV & Radio was the largest income source for creators.

The report gives context from Nielsen: in May 2026, streaming accounted for 48.6% of all TV viewing in the US, and YouTube alone for a record 13.8%. We wrote earlier this year that YouTube is now the world’s largest media company. Anyone who has looked at broadcast commissioning budgets lately knows the direction. Still, it is something different to see linear TV in third place in a global royalties table.

Audiovisual collections pass €750 million

Collections for the audiovisual repertoire, which means the authors of films and series, rose by 8.0% to €762 million. This is the fourth increase in a row, and the total is 42.3% above its 2016 level. Europe still dominates with 86.2% of the global total. France alone collected €273 million, more than a third of the world total.

Here too, part of the growth comes from new members. The Writers Guild of Japan and the Korea Television and Radio Writers Association reported to CISAC for the first time and added €64 million. My own calculation from the report’s figures: without those two new members, audiovisual collections would have been about 1% lower than in 2024, not 8% higher. CISAC does not give a like-for-like number for audiovisual, so please read this as my estimate. It does show that, in the established markets, collections for screenwriters and directors did not grow in 2025.

TV & Radio is still by far the largest source for audiovisual authors, with €462 million, or 60.7% of the total (up 0.5%). In France, TV & Radio collections fell by 9.7%. According to the report, this was because 2024 had unusually high payments and because a joint licensing agreement with TV distribution platforms was in renegotiation.

What streaming pays screenwriters and directors

Audiovisual collections from digital use grew for the seventh year in a row, by 32.0% to €142 million. The largest single increase came from Japan, with €30.2 million of new revenue. France accounted for 44.9% of digital audiovisual collections, as SACD continued to sign and renegotiate contracts with distributors. These include retroactive deals for HBO Max for the period 2024 to 2027, and for Paramount+ from 2022. In Uruguay, the society AGADU received its first payment from Netflix, which is also the first time that collections were made for screenwriters and directors in that country.

Not every negotiation ends in an agreement. SACD started legal action against TikTok in November 2025. According to the society, negotiations had not produced acceptable terms, and TikTok had not removed works at SACD’s request.

To put €142 million in context: Futuresource estimates that consumers spent around $142 billion on subscription video services in 2025. This is not a like-for-like comparison, because the societies collect only certain rights, in certain countries. But in my opinion, the gap between those two numbers explains why authors’ societies are so focused on streaming deals right now. (I hope the streamers’ licensing departments read page 41 of this report.)

Cinema recovers, but not to 2016

Cinema collections across all repertoires rose by 5.3% in 2025, to their highest level since 2019. They are still 10.2% below 2016, though. CISAC quotes Gower Street Analytics, which puts the global box office for 2025 at $33.6 billion, up 12%, with another increase forecast for 2026.

Futuresource notes in the report that original productions, familiar IP and theatrical releases remain the strongest draws for streamers. It names Netflix and Apple TV+ among the services that give selected films a cinema run before they go to streaming. With the Paramount and Warner Bros. merger promising 30 theatrical releases per year, it will be interesting to see whether cinema collections return to the 2016 level in the next report.

Music in films and series

For composers who write for film and TV, one detail in the report is relevant. In June 2026, CISAC launched AVR+, a machine-readable format for cue sheets based on the Global Cue Sheet Standard 2.0. Cue sheets list the music used in a film or TV program, and when that data is incomplete, societies cannot always identify the works and pay the royalties. AVR+ is meant to automate this and link the music use data more directly to payments. It also identifies the sound recordings, so performers and labels can benefit too.

The report uses Netflix’s KPop Demon Hunters as its example: the soundtrack song “Golden” generated 2.43 billion on-demand audio streams worldwide in 2025.

The subscription boom slows down

The section from Futuresource Consulting is, in my opinion, the most useful part of the report for anyone in production. Futuresource expects global spending on subscription video-on-demand to grow from around $142 billion in 2025 to $189 billion in 2030, and paid subscriptions from 2.2 billion to 2.6 billion. But annual growth falls from 14% in 2025 to low single digits by the end of the decade. In North America, 85% of households already subscribe to at least one service.

Platforms now earn more from each subscriber instead of finding new ones: video revenue per user in the 21 markets that Futuresource tracks was 16% higher in 2025 than in 2022. Between 2025 and 2026, at least one global streaming service raised the price of its ad-supported tier in 17 markets. Dave Watkins, Principal Analyst at Futuresource, puts it like this: “The next phase of growth will be won not by acquiring new audiences, but by deepening the value of the ones platforms already have.”

The report also says that bundles with telecom companies and pay-TV operators usually give up some revenue per user for scale and lower churn. When royalties depend on platform revenue, that is not good news for authors. That is my reading, not a claim from the report, but I am almost certain that the next licensing negotiations will be about exactly these bundles.

AI is in every foreword

All three forewords are about AI. CISAC President and ABBA co-founder Björn Ulvaeus writes: “Human creativity is not the enemy of artificial intelligence. It is the reason artificial intelligence exists.” Director General Gadi Oron adds in the press release: “But as we enter the age of AI, past growth cannot be taken for granted. Our priority must be to ensure that technology strengthens, rather than erodes, creators’ livelihoods.” In June, CISAC’s General Assembly in Paris adopted the Paris Commitment, which asks governments, technology companies and cultural industries to keep human creativity recognized, protected and fairly paid.

The report has one hard number on AI content, and it comes from music. Deezer reported that fully AI-generated tracks were 34% of the new tracks delivered to its service each day in November 2025, and more than half on peak days in June 2026. CISAC points out that these are upload numbers, not listening or royalty figures. According to Oron, the first licenses between authors’ societies and AI developers have started to appear.

What the report does not have is any figure for AI licensing income, and Futuresource writes that the scale and direction of AI’s impact on collections “remain difficult to assess.” For filmmakers, the debate is already concrete, from the backlash against Seedance 2.0 to A24’s deal with Google DeepMind and the copyright case against OpenAI. My guess is that next year’s report will have to put a number on it.

Where to get the report

The full CISAC Global Collections Report 2026 is free to download from the CISAC website in English, French and Spanish. The figures are based on the 2025 gross domestic collections of 228 CISAC members in 111 countries.

Do you receive royalties through an authors’ society for your films or series, and has streaming income made a difference for you? And should AI developers pay for training on audiovisual works through the same societies? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: SIRUI Aurora 15mm F1.6 and 24mm F1.4 Launched – Fast Full-Frame Autofocus Primes for Sony E and L-Mount
entry.summary: SIRUI has officially launched the Aurora 15mm F1.6 and 24mm F1.4, two fast full-frame autofocus primes that take its Aurora series to the wide end. Both lenses use an STM autofocus motor that works with the camera’s eye detection and subject tracking, an 11-blade aperture with a
entry.content:
SIRUI has officially launched the Aurora 15mm F1.6 and 24mm F1.4, two fast full-frame autofocus primes that take its Aurora series to the wide end. Both lenses use an STM autofocus motor that works with the camera’s eye detection and subject tracking, an 11-blade aperture with a switchable click/de-click ring, an iris lock, a programmable Fn button, a USB-C port for firmware updates and a dust- and splash-resistant all-metal body. The Sony E and L-Mount versions are available for pre-order now, and Nikon Z and FUJIFILM X versions follow in Q1 2027.

We saw pre-production samples of both lenses at SIRUI’s booth in Amsterdam and reported on them in our IBC 2026 first look. Back then, SIRUI’s Sonny Liu spoke of a price of $500 to $600 per lens and of availability “in the next couple of months.” SIRUI kept that promise quite precisely: the final prices sit at the two ends of that range, and the launch came less than two months after the show.

The Aurora series started in October 2024 with the 85mm F1.4, which Johnnie reviewed on the Sony a1 II. The 35mm F1.4 followed in September 2025. With the two new wides, the series now has four focal lengths from 15mm to 85mm. L-Mount is a launch mount this time because SIRUI joined the L-Mount Alliance in March 2025.

Aurora 15mm F1.6: wide and fast

The 15mm F1.6 is the more unusual of the two lenses. Its optical design has 17 elements in 12 groups, with three aspherical, three ED and three HRI (high refractive index) elements. On a full-frame sensor, it covers a diagonal angle of view of 109.3°. SIRUI states that optical distortion is controlled to approximately 1.4%. The company does not say how much of this comes from the optics and how much from in-camera correction, so this is a figure I want to see in a test before I trust it for architecture work.

SIRUI markets the F1.6 aperture against the F1.8 that many fast ultra-wides use, with about 27% more light in theory. That is one-third of a stop. It is not a large difference, but the lens is also wider than the many 16mm F1.8 options, such as the Viltrox AF 16mm F1.8 for L-Mount. For astrophotography, night exteriors and dark interiors, every bit of light helps.

For video shooters, the most practical detail is the 77mm (M77x0.75) front filter thread. Many ultra-wides at this focal length have a bulbous front element and need a filter holder system, so a standard screw-in ND or polarizer is a real advantage on a gimbal. The minimum focus distance is 0.3m (0.98ft), with a maximum magnification of 0.08x. The lens has a maximum diameter of 82mm (3.23in). The Sony E version is 106.4mm (4.19in) long and weighs 542g (1.19lb); the L-Mount version is 104.4mm (4.11in) long and weighs 550g (1.21lb).

Aurora 24mm F1.4: the classic wide

The 24mm F1.4 uses 14 elements in 11 groups, with three aspherical, four ED and three HRI elements. The diagonal angle of view is 82.93°. The minimum focus distance is 0.26m (0.85ft), and the maximum magnification of 0.15x (1:6.67) is useful for close details and product shots.

The 24mm takes 62mm (M62x0.75) filters and has a maximum diameter of 76mm (2.99in). It is not a small lens for a 24mm F1.4: the Sony E version is 106.6mm (4.20in) long and weighs 550g (1.21lb), and the L-Mount version is 104.6mm (4.12in) long and weighs 560g (1.23lb). The two new lenses are almost the same length. My feeling is that SIRUI did this on purpose, so that you can swap them on a gimbal without a full rebalance, but that’s just my guess.

The price is interesting. At $499, the 24mm F1.4 costs less than the Aurora 35mm F1.4, which SIRUI sells for $549 in its own store.

Same controls across the series

Both lenses have the same set of controls as the 35mm and 85mm. There is an AF/MF switch, a click on/off switch for the aperture ring, an iris lock that holds the ring in the A position or in the manual aperture range, and an Fn button that is set to AF lock by default and can be assigned to other functions. A USB-C port on the barrel is for firmware updates. Both lenses have an all-metal build with dust-, stain- and splash-resistant protection, and each comes with a lens hood.

According to SIRUI, the STM motor gives fast, accurate and quiet autofocus, and both lenses have low focus breathing. We have not tested this yet. SIRUI also publishes a Sony camera compatibility list: most current bodies are compatible in photo and video mode, but the a6000, for example, is only partially compatible in video mode. Check the list before you order for an older body.

SIRUI gives a three-year replacement warranty on both lenses: within three years of purchase, a lens with a failure that does not come from misuse is replaced free of charge. In the box, you get the lens, a lens pouch, the hood, and front and rear caps.

What about Nikon Z and FUJIFILM X?

The Aurora 35mm and 85mm are already available in Nikon Z and FUJIFILM X mount, and SIRUI says that both new lenses follow in these two mounts in Q1 2027. On an APS-C body with a 1.5x crop, the 15mm gives a field of view similar to a 23mm lens on full frame, and the 24mm one similar to a 36mm lens. (And while you are at it, SIRUI, a matching 50mm would make this a complete set.)

Price and availability

The SIRUI Aurora 15mm F1.6 costs $599 and the Aurora 24mm F1.4 costs $499. In Europe, SIRUI lists the lenses at €649 and €539, including VAT. Both are available for pre-order now in Sony E and L-Mount from retailers and from SIRUI’s store (15mm F1.6, 24mm F1.4). The Nikon Z and FUJIFILM X versions are scheduled for Q1 2027.

Do you already shoot with the Aurora 35mm or 85mm, and will the 15mm or 24mm fill a gap in your kit? Or is a fast ultra-wide with a front filter thread more important to you than autofocus? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: Flanders Scientific VP and V Series Introduced – Seven QD-OLED Monitors, Up to 4,000 Nits, 12G-SDI and 3D
entry.summary: Flanders Scientific has announced seven new QD-OLED monitors in two new lines, the VP Series and the V Series. They use the same panels, the same color engine and the same GaiaColor calibration tools as the flagship XMP monitors, but they leave out the onboard scopes, Look LUTs a
entry.content:
Flanders Scientific has announced seven new QD-OLED monitors in two new lines, the VP Series and the V Series. They use the same panels, the same color engine and the same GaiaColor calibration tools as the flagship XMP monitors, but they leave out the onboard scopes, Look LUTs and Livegrade integration. The result is a much lower price, plus one feature that the XMP never had: stereoscopic 3D.

This launch comes about seven months after Atomos announced the acquisition of Flanders Scientific (FSI) in April, and I think it tells us a lot about where the two companies want to take the brand. FSI CEO Bram Desmet and Atomos CEO Peter Barber explain the new lineup together in a video on the FSI channel. The idea is simple: many grading suites, post houses and VFX rooms pay for XMP features they never touch, because they run a standalone scope and do not need processed monitor outputs. FSI now gives those users the same image for less money. According to the company, the VP Series costs up to 30% less than the matching XMP models, and the V Series up to 48% less. The XMP and XMP C monitors stay in full production as the flagship models.

We have covered FSI for years, from the DM160 OLED to the 31.5-inch XMP310 QD-OLED. So the question for this launch is not the image quality. The question is which features you can live without.

Seven monitors, two lines

The VP Series is the line with professional SDI connectivity. It has four models: the VP270 (26.5-inch, 1,000 nits), the VP310 (31.5-inch, 1,000 nits), the VP551 (55-inch, 4,000 nits) and the VP651 (65-inch, 4,000 nits). FSI says it designed this line with the post house in mind, where professional inputs and color accuracy are essential, but where a separate scope solution already does the measuring.

The V Series drops SDI completely and connects through HDMI 2.1 and DisplayPort 1.4 only. It has three models: the V270 (26.5-inch, 1,000 nits), the V310 (31.5-inch, 1,000 nits) and the V550 (55-inch, 2,000 nits). FSI sees it in the rooms around the main grading suite, such as VFX, editorial, animation, game development and audio post, and as the lowest-priced entry point into FSI QD-OLED monitoring for colorists who work over HDMI or DisplayPort.

Every model uses a 3840 x 2160 10-bit QD-OLED panel with a 179-degree viewing angle, the same panel as the XMP model of the same size and peak luminance. That is the most important point of the whole announcement for me. If a facility runs an XMP in the main suite and a V Series in the edit bay next door, both screens use the same panel technology and the same color management system. According to FSI, this is what keeps the picture consistent from room to room.

What the VP Series offers

The VP models have four 12G-SDI inputs, and each input has its own clean SDI loop output. Single, dual and quad-link connections are supported, and FSI lists signals up to 8K UHD and 8K DCI at 12-bit 4:4:4 over quad 12G or 6G links, scaled to the native UHD panel. HDMI 2.1 and DisplayPort 1.4 inputs with up to 120Hz signal support are there for secondary sources. The monitors read the SDI payload ID (VPID) and set 4:4:4 or 4:2:2, 10 or 12-bit, and RGB or YCbCr automatically, with a manual override when the payload ID is missing or wrong.

Quad View mode shows up to four inputs on screen at once, and it does not need genlock, only sources at the same frame rate. Each input can also have its own gamut, EOTF, white point and luminance settings, all visible at the same time. For multi-camera review or a side-by-side of two grades, that is a very practical tool.

The two large VP models are the ones that will get the most attention. The VP551 and VP651 reach about 4,000 nits at an 18% window, about 2,200 nits at 32% and about 400 nits full screen, with a contrast ratio of about 8,000,000:1 and about 90% coverage of Rec.2020. FSI says both qualify as Dolby Vision mastering monitors, and it pitches them as single-screen solutions where the colorist and the client look at the same display. The 26.5-inch and 31.5-inch VP models reach about 1,000 nits at an 18% window, with about 1,500,000:1 contrast and about 80% of Rec.2020, and FSI also lists them as Dolby Vision mastering monitors.

What you lose compared to the XMP

FSI is open about the cuts. The VP and V Series have no waveform, no vectorscope, no Look LUT support, and no Pomfort Livegrade or Assimilate Live Assist integration. The VP models also have no processed SDI outputs (only clean loops), and the front keypad and rotary knobs of the XMP are gone. Instead, there is a simple 5-way controller on the back of the monitor. If your monitor sits in a grading room and you drive it mostly through the remote software, that is probably not a big loss. On a DIT cart, where you change settings all day, I would miss the front controls.

What stays is the core FSI feature set. That includes GaiaColor AutoCal, which profiles the panel once with a probe connected directly to the monitor and then derives all color space selections from that profile, without a computer. The GaiaColor Analyzer runs a QC check of the calibration in as little as 60 seconds and shows the report on screen, and the free IP Remote Utility exports it as a PDF. Calman and ColourSpace calibration LUTs are also supported. Then there are LUM Coloring false color with a nits-based scale in PQ mode, red, green and blue-only modes, the standard and custom markers, 1:1 pixel mapping and accurate interlaced monitoring.

Remote control works over Ethernet with the IP Remote Utility for Mac, Windows and iOS (with Elgato Stream Deck support), over RS-485 serial, with the optional R-RS wireless remote, and through GPI contact closure with up to seven assignable functions. You can also save up to five configurations and switch between them with one button press.

The V Series: QD-OLED over HDMI and DisplayPort

For many of our readers, the V Series is probably the more interesting line. The V270 and V310 bring the XMP270 and XMP310 panels to an HDMI and DisplayPort workflow, and the V550 uses the 2,000-nit 55-inch panel of the XMP550 with about 4,000,000:1 contrast. Inputs are one HDMI 2.1 and one DisplayPort 1.4 port, plus a 3.5mm headphone output and optical S/PDIF.

Interestingly, the XMP and XMP C monitors have no HDMI input at all, so the new lines are actually the first FSI QD-OLED monitors with HDMI 2.1. My guess is that this will make the V Series attractive for colorists and editors who already monitor through an HDMI output card or interface from their grading system, but that is just my guess. The trade-off is clear: no SDI, no Quad View and no clean loop outputs.

Stereo 3D is back

Both new lines support stereoscopic 3D, which the XMP series never did. The VP models accept 3D over HDMI and dual-link SDI. It works with an optional active 3D system: a 3D sync module that connects to the monitor and a pair of active shutter glasses, sold as a bundle for $250. FSI itself calls 3D a niche requirement, but it also says that few professional monitors still support it and that there is demand. Anyone who has to deliver or QC 3D versions of feature films or immersive content will know how short that list is.

Power, weight and mounting

All seven models have an aluminum chassis and a fanless design with a graphite heat sink, so they make no fan noise in the suite. The 26.5-inch and 31.5-inch models use an external 100-240V AC power supply and also have a 3-pin XLR DC input (24V, up to 36V supported), so they can run from a battery or a cart. They draw about 35W to 220W and have 100mm VESA mounting. The 26.5-inch models weigh 5.9kg (13.1 lb) without the desktop feet, the 31.5-inch models 7.2kg (16.0 lb).

The 55-inch and 65-inch models have an internal AC supply (IEC C14), draw about 75W to 325W and use 300 x 200mm VESA mounting. The VP551 and V550 weigh 17.7kg (39 lb) without feet, and the VP651 weighs 23.0kg (50.8 lb).

Where does this leave the XMP, and Atomos?

The price gap is significant. The VP270 costs $3,500 less than the XMP270, and the V270 costs $5,500 less. At the top, the VP651 costs $6,500 less than the XMP651 with the same 4,000-nit panel. In my opinion, that makes the large VP models very attractive for client rooms that want a true HDR mastering display without the full XMP feature set.

Peter Barber, Managing Director and CEO of Atomos, explains the reasoning in the press release: “Traditionally, the cost of high-end reference monitors has limited how widely they could be deployed across post-production facilities. By offering the same exceptional image quality, colour accuracy and calibration capabilities at a more accessible price point, we are making it possible for customers to equip more workstations, more editing suites and more production environments with professional reference monitoring.” For a facility with many rooms, the savings add up per room, and I think that is the real target of this launch.

It is also interesting to look at this from the Atomos side. When Atomos showed the Studio Pro 2710, it positioned it as a reference monitor below $10,000. Now FSI, a company in the same group, sells a 26.5-inch QD-OLED with the XMP panel for $5,995. In our interview with Peter Barber at NAB 2026, he spoke about building a monitoring ecosystem from camera to grading suite, and I am almost certain that the VP and V Series are part of that plan, but that is just my feeling. At the other end of the market, QD-OLED monitors with SDI inputs such as the ASUS ProArt PA32USD sell for much less. They do not offer FSI’s calibration system, its 4,000-nit large-screen options or its facility support, but they show how fast the prices in this category are moving. (And FSI, a V310 review unit on my desk would be very welcome.)

Price and availability

According to Flanders Scientific, both series begin shipping in November 2026, and the FSI store currently lists a delivery time of two weeks after order. US prices for the VP Series are $7,995 for the VP270, $8,995 for the VP310, $15,995 for the VP551 and $17,495 for the VP651.

The V Series costs $5,995 for the V270, $6,995 for the V310 and $12,495 for the V550. The optional 3D sync module and active 3D glasses bundle costs $250. FSI has its own sales and service operations in Europe and the UK, but European prices have not been announced yet, and the new models are not yet listed at CVP at the time of writing. You can find all details on the Flanders Scientific website.

Do you need scopes and Look LUTs on your reference monitor, or does a separate scope already do that job in your suite? Would a V Series monitor over HDMI be enough for your grading work? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: Deity PR-2ii Pocket Recorder Released – Dual-ADC Preamp, IP54 Sealing, and WAV File Recovery
entry.summary: Deity has released the PR-2ii, the second generation of its PR-2 pocket recorder, the small two-AA box that many sound recordists hide on talent as a backup for their wireless. The new model gets a dual-ADC preamp that Deity says lowers self-noise by 5.4 dB, an IP54 dust and spla
entry.content:
Deity has released the PR-2ii, the second generation of its PR-2 pocket recorder, the small two-AA box that many sound recordists hide on talent as a backup for their wireless. The new model gets a dual-ADC preamp that Deity says lowers self-noise by 5.4 dB, an IP54 dust and splash rated housing, a PSRAM buffer with WAV file recovery, a brighter color screen, and microSD support up to 1TB. It is available now at B&H as a bundle with Deity’s Avora lavalier microphone.

Pocket recorders are not the most exciting products we cover, but they are often the ones that save the take when a wireless link drops out behind a wall or in a crowd. Deity first showed the PR-2ii with production firmware at IBC 2026 in Amsterdam in September, together with its new TC-2 timecode box and the THEOS D4RX four-channel receiver. At the same show, we gave our Best-of-Show award in the audio category to the Deity PR-4, so I was curious to see what the company would do with its smallest recorder. The answer: the concept stays the same (one 3.5mm input, two tracks, two AA batteries), but almost everything inside has been revised.

What changed from the PR-2?

The main change is the preamp. The PR-2ii uses two acquisition paths within the analog input channel with 32-bit conversion, and Deity rates the internal-recording dynamic range at 124 dB or higher, compared with 123 dB typical for the PR-2 in 32-bit float. Equivalent input noise is specified at -117 dBV (A-weighted, 36 dB gain, 150 ohm source). The PR-2 spec sheet gives -130 dBu at a different gain setting and in a different unit, so the two EIN figures cannot be compared directly. The comparison to look at is Deity’s own claim of 5.4 dB lower self-noise, and that is a manufacturer figure, not one we have measured.

Storage support goes from microSDHC cards up to 128GB on the PR-2 to microSD cards up to 1TB. The USB-C port also does more now. On the PR-2, it worked as a card reader and for firmware updates. On the PR-2ii, it adds USB Audio Class 2.0 class-compliant operation as a two-channel, 48 kHz, 24-bit sound card, plus timecode output. The screen is a 600-nit color TFT, which Deity says is 60% brighter than the one on the PR-2.

Two things have not moved forward. Recording is still 48 kHz only, and 32-bit float is still mono only, so a stereo recording (two lavs, or a stereo feed from a mixer) is 24-bit integer. I would have liked to see two-channel 32-bit float this time (Deity, if you are reading this, that is the first item on my wish list for a PR-3). Rated battery life also goes down on paper: the PR-2 was rated at up to 30 hours with lithium AA batteries, the PR-2ii at 20+ hours with Deity’s AA batteries. Deity connects this figure to the brighter display. My guess is that the new preamp needs some power too, but that is only a guess.

Built for the recorder you cannot reach

For a recorder that lives under wardrobe or inside a car, the protection features are the most practical part of the update. A PSRAM buffer holds audio on its way to the card and evens out differences in write speed, so according to Deity, the PR-2ii works with a wider range of microSD cards. If a recording stops unexpectedly or a file is corrupted, you switch the recorder back on and it writes the missing WAV file footer and recovers the file. Anyone who has lost a file because a battery lost contact in the middle of a take will understand why this matters.

The housing is now IP54 rated against dust and splashes, with a new rubber gasket around the battery compartment. A 6H tempered-glass cover protects the screen, and the controls are buttons, which Deity says make the front stronger than on the previous model. The specified operating range is -20 to 60°C (-4 to 140°F) at 0 to 90% relative humidity, non-condensing.

Faster setup for small crews

Deity has added gain presets for popular lavaliers: the DPA 4060/4061, Sennheiser MKE 2, Countryman B3, and Shure TL47. They give you a practical starting level without a sound check. Input gain runs from -12 dB to +36 dB in both mic and line mode, the maximum input level is -0.5 dBu (0.73 Vrms), and the 3.5mm TRS input supplies 5V plug-in power for the microphone.

The rest of the toolset covers what a run-and-gun shooter needs: 75 Hz and 150 Hz low-cut filters, a soft-knee limiter with a fixed -6 dBFS threshold (0.75 ms attack, 1000 ms release), onboard noise reduction, pre-record, and mark points to find important moments later in post. One-touch recording uses a dedicated record button. In 32-bit float mode, the gain setting is less critical, of course, but the presets still help in 24-bit stereo mode and for the headphone feed.

Timecode and remote control

The PR-2ii receives wireless timecode from Deity’s own ecosystem, which includes the TC-1 timecode box and TC-SL1 slate, the THEOS wireless system, the PR-4, and other PR-2ii units. Deity specifies the Bluetooth LE timecode range at 80 to 95 m (260 to 310 ft) and the drift at one frame every 48 hours. The 3.5mm output takes timecode in or out during recording, as LTC (3V) or ATC, and USB-C timecode output works with XTRA, DJI, and Insta360 cameras, according to Deity.

Control runs through the Sidus Audio app on iPhone, iPad, Android, and macOS. From the app, you can start and stop recording, check status, and change settings at up to 76 m (250 ft), the same control range Deity quoted for the PR-2. Over Bluetooth, the app also lets you listen to the recorder from more than 40 m (130 ft) away. For a solo shooter with the recorder hidden on talent, that means you can check the audio without walking over and reaching under a jacket.

Size, power, and what is in the box

The PR-2ii measures 60 x 58.5 x 18.5mm (2.36 x 2.30 x 0.73in) and weighs 55g (1.9oz) without batteries; the removable back clip adds about 3.5g. Power comes from two AA batteries (1.5V maximum each) or from 5V over USB-C. Deity gives the power consumption as up to 0.53 W on AA batteries and up to 0.71 W on USB-C power. Files are recorded as BWF WAV and are split at approximately 4GB, and the headphone output delivers 62.5 mW at 16 ohms.

Where does this fit in the market? 32-bit float pocket recorders are not new: the Tascam DR-10L Pro and Zoom’s F2 work in the same category, and many wireless transmitters now record internally as well. In my opinion, Deity’s advantage is less the recorder itself and more the system around it. If you already use a TC-1, a PR-4, or THEOS transmitters, the PR-2ii simply joins the same timecode network and the same app.

Price and availability

The Deity PR-2ii is available now at B&H for $259, bundled with the Avora lavalier microphone. At the time of writing, CVP lists only the original PR-2, and Deity directs European buyers to its local dealers, so a euro price is not available yet. More information is on the Deity website.

Do you still put a pocket recorder on talent as a backup for your wireless, or do you rely on the internal recording in your transmitters now? Would file recovery and IP54 sealing make you upgrade from the original PR-2? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: Thomas Riedel Honored at Camerimage 2026 for Preserving European Film Technology With ARRI Acquisition
entry.summary: ARRI owner Thomas Riedel has been honored for preserving European film technology: he received a European Film Industry Preservation Award at the opening gala of the 34th ToruńCAMERIMAGE International Film Festival in Toruń, Poland, on Saturday, November 7, 2026. According to RIE
entry.content:
ARRI owner Thomas Riedel has been honored for preserving European film technology: he received a European Film Industry Preservation Award at the opening gala of the 34th ToruńCAMERIMAGE International Film Festival in Toruń, Poland, on Saturday, November 7, 2026. According to RIEDEL Communications, the festival honored him for his dedication to the European film industry, and the company links the award directly to his acquisition of ARRI earlier this year. For a man who comes from intercoms and live broadcast infrastructure, this is quite a welcome from the cinematography community.

I have to admit, I did not expect to write about Thomas Riedel and Camerimage in the same headline when he bought ARRI in April. Camerimage is the festival of the art of cinematography, and its audience is DPs, camera assistants and gaffers, not broadcast engineers. But the trophy plate says it clearly: “Thomas Riedel, ARRI, European Film Industry Preservation Award, CAMERIMAGE 2026”. RIEDEL Communications shared the news and the photos on LinkedIn, with the comment that “with this year’s acquisition of ARRI, he is sending a strong signal in support of innovation and the preservation of European film technology.”

What the award is for

At the time of writing, the festival website does not list the award or give a written citation, so the information comes from RIEDEL Communications and from the trophy itself. The trophy is a golden frog statuette on a black stone base. The frog is the symbol of Camerimage, and the festival’s main competition prize is the Golden Frog. My reading of the award’s name is simple: the festival sees the sale of ARRI to a German entrepreneur, and not to a financial investor or a large non-European corporation, as a contribution to keeping European film technology in European hands. That is my interpretation, as the festival has not published its reasons yet.

That reading fits what we reported when the deal was announced. In our article on the acquisition, we described how the Stahl family, heirs of ARRI co-founder Robert Richter, ran an international bidding process for the 109-year-old Munich company. Thomas Riedel bought ARRI as sole owner of the Riedel Group, with his own capital. ARRI kept its independent operations, its headquarters in Munich and its management team under Managing Directors Chris Richter and David Bermbach.

Seven months of ARRI under Riedel

The award comes after a busy first half year. In May, ARRI and Riedel worked together at the Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna, where 24 ARRI ALEXA 35 Live cameras ran on Riedel infrastructure, and we went behind the scenes there. In July, ARRI sold its global rental business to the division’s management, backed by H2 Equity Partners. Riedel had already told us at NAB 2026 that he did not strongly believe in a model where a manufacturer sells cameras to rental houses and competes with them at the same time.

Much of the first year has been about live production, which is where Riedel is strongest. That is why I find the Camerimage award interesting. It puts the focus back on the part of ARRI that cinematographers care about most: the ALEXA cameras, the lenses and the lighting used on feature films. My feeling is that this is also a message from the festival to the new owner: the cinema community expects ARRI to stay a cinema company first (Thomas, if you are reading this, I think a lot of DPs in Toruń would agree with me).

Camerimage 2026

The 34th edition of the festival runs from November 7 to 14, 2026 in Toruń. Last year, the festival was still called EnergaCAMERIMAGE; this year, it carries the name of its host city, ToruńCAMERIMAGE. Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial”, shot by Malik Hassan Sayeed, opened the festival after the gala. ARRI has been a fixture at the festival for many years; last year, it ran a daily workshop series at its booth. If you have never been to Toruń, our complete guide to Camerimage 2025 gives a good idea of what the week looks like, from the workshops to the main competition. More information on this year’s program is on the official Camerimage website, and more about the company is on the RIEDEL website and the ARRI website.

Do you see the award as recognition of a deal that kept ARRI in European hands, or is it too early to judge what Thomas Riedel will do with the company? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: Canon Camera Control Centre Announced – Free Multi-Camera Software for PTZ and Cinema EOS, Up to 200 Cameras
entry.summary: Canon has announced Camera Control Centre, a free computer application that puts setup, PTZ control, color matching, firmware updates and batch settings for up to 200 Canon cameras into one window. It replaces four separate Canon tools, adds a four-camera Quick Adjustments view,
entry.content:
Canon has announced Camera Control Centre, a free computer application that puts setup, PTZ control, color matching, firmware updates and batch settings for up to 200 Canon cameras into one window. It replaces four separate Canon tools, adds a four-camera Quick Adjustments view, an angle-of-view simulator and saved multicam setups, and it supports Canon’s PTZ cameras as well as the EOS C400, C80, C50 and other Cinema EOS models. The Windows 11 version is due in early January 2027, with macOS to follow.

Canon announced Camera Control Centre on November 4, and at first glance it reads like a pure broadcast and PTZ story. I think it is more relevant than that for many of our readers, because the supported device list also includes Cinema EOS cameras, and more and more small productions, live streams and corporate events now mix a Canon PTZ camera or two with an EOS C80 or a C50. Until now, such a Canon system needed up to four different applications: the Camera Search Tool for initial setup, the Remote Camera Control Application for PTZ control and presets, the Multi-Camera Management Application for firmware updates and camera settings, and the Camera Colour Matching Application for LUT-based color matching. According to Canon Europe, Camera Control Centre merges all four into one workflow, from planning and first setup to operation and maintenance.

This comes in the same week as Canon’s December firmware update for the EOS C400, C80 and C50, which adds Multi Matrix color control, a feature Canon pitches for matching Cinema EOS feeds with studio cameras in live production. The direction is clear: Canon wants its cinema bodies and its PTZ line (we covered the CR-N350 and CR-N400 last year) to work as one multi-camera system.

Four apps become one

Canon’s English screenshots show how the application is organized. A Devices section holds the registered cameras and the Multicam Setups. The Shooting section has Camera Operations, Presets, Auto Tracking, Quick Image Adjust and Monitoring, and a Tools section has Color Matching and FOV Calculation. The camera operation screen combines a PTZ panel with image settings, focus, crop and auto tracking controls, and you can select several cameras and operate them together. According to Canon Japan’s product page, the video view can show 1×1, 2×2, 3×3 or 1×4 layouts.

Canon says that the software connects to up to 200 compatible devices over its XC Protocol. That number is about device management, not about 200 live images on one screen. For larger installations, the more interesting part is batch maintenance: you can copy settings from one camera to many in real time, save a settings file and load it into other cameras later, and run firmware updates or restarts on several cameras at once from a single list page.

What is new: Quick Adjustments, FOV Calculation and Multicam Setups

On top of the merged functions, Canon adds three new tools. Quick Adjustments puts the previews and adjustment panels of up to four cameras on one screen, so you can compare the images and adjust shutter speed, white balance, iris and gain without a hardware controller for each camera. Each thumbnail can also switch to color bars, and if you watch the feeds on external monitors, you can hide the thumbnails and keep only the adjustment panels.

FOV Calculation simulates the angle of view of a Canon remote camera before you install it. You enter the camera model, the distance to the subject and the zoom position, and the application shows how a person of a given height (for example 175cm / 5 ft 9 in) will appear in the frame, without any camera hardware. For anyone who plans a lecture hall, a studio or a church installation with ceiling-mounted PTZ cameras, that is a practical tool, because moving a camera after the installation is expensive.

Multicam Setups saves the settings of several cameras, including image quality settings, per scene or per program, and recalls them the next time you use the same setup. Groups of devices can also be backed up and restored together.

Color matching, with limits

The color matching function comes from the existing Camera Colour Matching Application. You capture a still image of a color chart from a reference camera and from the target camera, and the software automatically adjusts the target camera’s color to the reference and sends a LUT to it. Canon Japan lists the requirements in detail. The target camera must be able to store a LUT over the XC Protocol, and at launch this means only the CR-N700, CR-N400 and CR-N350 PTZ cameras. The reference camera can be from any manufacturer, as long as it outputs BT.709 or HDR at 2K resolution or higher. Cinema EOS cameras are supported in this workflow only as the reference camera.

To get the images into the computer, you need either a video capture device with SDI or HDMI input, or Canon’s RC-IP1000 remote controller. Canon has confirmed the Blackmagic Design UltraStudio Recorder 3G (for 2K) and UltraStudio 4K Mini (for 4K) as capture devices with the CR-N700, CR-N400 and CR-N350. Supported charts are grid-type charts such as a Macbeth chart, the ColorChecker Video, and DSC Labs’ ChromaMatch Vista Std 709/2022 and CalMAlign ChromaDuMonde 24 + 4R. So, the typical case is clear: your A camera, for example an EOS C400 or a camera from another brand, is the reference, and the PTZ cameras follow it. I would love to see this work in the other direction too, with LUTs sent to Cinema EOS bodies (Canon, your Cinema EOS cameras already speak the XC Protocol, after all).

Which cameras are supported?

According to Canon Japan’s product page, Camera Control Centre supports the following devices at launch:

  • PTZ cameras: CR-N700, CR-N500, CR-X300, CR-N400, CR-N350, CR-N300 and CR-N100
  • Cinema and video cameras: EOS C500 Mark II, EOS C300 Mark III, EOS C400, EOS C80, EOS C70, EOS C50 and XF605
  • Remote controllers: RC-IP1000 and RC-IP300

Canon notes that the available functions vary by model. The application identifies which functions each camera supports, and settings follow each product’s specifications. My guess is that the cinema cameras will get mainly setup, image settings and the four-feed adjustment view, while full PTZ operation stays with the remote cameras, but Canon has not published a function list per model yet.

If you are shopping for one of the supported Cinema EOS bodies, the EOS C50 is available at B&H and CVP, the EOS C80 at B&H and CVP, and the EOS C400 at B&H and CVP.

Where does it fit?

Camera Control Centre is clearly built for broadcasters, education, corporate and public sector users who run several Canon PTZ cameras from one desk, and for them, one application instead of four is a real simplification. For cinema camera users, the value is smaller but still there: a free way to configure, adjust and maintain a mixed Canon fleet from a computer. It runs on a computer, though, not on a phone or tablet. For iPhone and iPad control, Canon already has its Multi-Camera Control app, and third-party apps such as Director Mode now put Canon and Sony cameras on one iPad screen. Sony goes a different route with its DP7 and DP5 camera control monitors, and FUJIFILM’s ETERNA ProRemote app controls up to four GFX ETERNA 55 cameras from an iPad.

The one thing I miss at launch is a Mac version. Canon says macOS will follow, but many productions run their video village from a MacBook, and the current Remote Camera Control Application already exists for macOS (so, Canon, please do not make Mac users wait too long).

Price and availability

Camera Control Centre is free. Canon Europe says that the download will be available from January 2027, and Canon Japan specifies early January, first for Windows 11, with macOS support to follow. Canon U.S.A., which calls the application Camera Control Center, said in its own announcement that it launches “later this year”, so the exact date may vary by region. The application interface is in English and Japanese, and Canon Japan lists the manual in English, Japanese, Simplified Chinese, French, German, Italian and Spanish. More details are on the Canon Japan product page and in the Canon Asia press release.

Do you run Canon PTZ cameras next to Cinema EOS bodies, and would one free application for setup, color matching and control change your workflow? Or do you need the Mac version first? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: Portkeys OVF-Z380 Eyepiece Kit Released for Sony PXW-Z380/Z300 – Flip-Up Optical Loupe, -3 to +8 Diopter
entry.summary: Portkeys has released the OVF-Z380, an optical eyepiece kit for the Sony PXW-Z380 and PXW-Z300 camcorders. The loupe clips onto the camera’s LCD and turns it into an eye-level viewfinder, with a -3 to +8 diopter, an adjustable silicone eyecup, and an internal dust-proof structure
entry.content:
Portkeys has released the OVF-Z380, an optical eyepiece kit for the Sony PXW-Z380 and PXW-Z300 camcorders. The loupe clips onto the camera’s LCD and turns it into an eye-level viewfinder, with a -3 to +8 diopter, an adjustable silicone eyecup, and an internal dust-proof structure. A flip-up design moves it out of the way when the operator needs the touchscreen.

Sony’s PXW-Z300 has no built-in viewfinder. When Sony announced the PXW-Z300 in July 2025, the handheld XDCAM camcorder came with 1/2-inch 4K 3-CMOS Exmor R sensors, a 17x zoom lens, an electronic variable ND filter, and C2PA content authentication, but operators frame on a 3.5-inch LCD only. Accessory makers have since offered optical loupes for that screen. We reported on the Zacuto Z-Finder for the PXW-Z300 one week after the camera’s launch, and on the Vocas EL-40 Eyepiece Loupe at IBC 2026. The Portkeys OVF-Z380 is a third option, and it comes from a company that is better known for its on-camera monitors.

A loupe for the Z300’s LCD

The OVF-Z380 is a passive optical viewfinder. It has no display and no electronics of its own. According to Portkeys, it mounts on the camera’s LCD with a screen mount that the operator releases with a button on the bottom of the unit. In the lowered position, the operator looks at the camcorder’s own screen through the loupe’s optics. The flip-up design lifts the loupe off the screen, so the touchscreen stays available for menus, playback, and low-angle shots without removing the kit from the camera. Portkeys says that installation and removal are quick.

An eyepiece also gives the operator a third point of contact with the camera, together with both hands. For news and documentary crews who shoot handheld in bright daylight, that is often the main reason to use a loupe on a camcorder that ships without a viewfinder. We discussed this in more detail in our article Welcome Back, EVF – We’ve Missed You!.

Diopter, eyecup and dust protection

The diopter adjusts from -3 to +8. That range covers many operators who would otherwise wear glasses behind the eyecup, especially farsighted ones. The eyecup is made of soft silicone, and Portkeys says that its orientation can be adjusted.

Dust on the optics or on the LCD is a common problem with loupes, because any particle between the eye and the screen shows up magnified. Portkeys addresses this with an internal dust-proof structure that includes a dust-protection glass between the screen mount and the optics, and with a removable dust cap that protects the eyepiece when the kit is not in use.

Size, weight and construction

The housing is made of ABS, glass, and aluminum alloy. The OVF-Z380 measures 156 x 99 x 71mm / 6.1 x 3.9 x 2.8in and weighs 282.6g (10oz). For comparison, Vocas gives a weight of 385g (13.6oz) for its complete EL-40 kit for the Z300, which includes a friction bracket for the camera’s LCD arm. Zacuto’s Z-Finder for the Z300 also uses a bracket that locks two of the arm’s three axes and mechanically strengthens it.

Current limitations

Portkeys does not publish a magnification figure for the OVF-Z380, and the product information does not list the box contents. Portkeys also does not say whether the kit includes a support for the Z300’s LCD arm, which Vocas and Zacuto supply with their loupes. Zacuto states 2.5x magnification for its Z-Finder. Operators who compare the three options should check these points before they buy.

The OVF-Z380 is not the first link between Portkeys and this camcorder. With the Portkeys firmware update for nine monitors in March 2026, the company added Wi-Fi and USB-C camera control for the PXW-Z380 to monitors such as the LH7P, LS7P, and BM5 IV WR. We last covered the company in September, when it introduced the Portkeys LH5P III monitor.

Price and availability

The Portkeys OVF-Z380 eyepiece kit is listed at B&H for $299. CVP does not list the kit at the time of writing. For comparison, Vocas sells the EL-40 with its Z300 attachment for €779, excluding VAT. More information is available on the Portkeys OVF-Z380 product page.
