Do you shoot with the Sony PXW-Z300 or PXW-Z380, and do you frame on the LCD or through a loupe? Would a lower price and weight be more important to you than a support bracket for the screen arm? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: Director Mode App Released for iPhone and iPad – Four-Camera Monitoring, REC ALL, and USB-C Control for Canon and Sony
entry.summary: Director Mode is a new iPhone and iPad app that monitors and controls selected Canon and Sony cameras, and it can show up to four of them side by side, even when you mix the two brands. The app comes from a small team in Florence, Italy, connects over Wi-Fi, LAN or a direct USB-C
entry.content:
Director Mode is a new iPhone and iPad app that monitors and controls selected Canon and Sony cameras, and it can show up to four of them side by side, even when you mix the two brands. The app comes from a small team in Florence, Italy, connects over Wi-Fi, LAN or a direct USB-C cable, and adds a waveform, focus peaking, custom LUTs and a REC ALL button in its Pro version. Director Mode Basic is free, and Pro is a one-time in-app purchase.

We see a lot of camera control apps, but almost all of them stay inside one brand. Canon has its apps for Canon bodies, Sony has its apps for Sony bodies, and if you run a Canon EOS C50 next to a Sony a7 V on a small documentary or interview shoot, you normally end up with two phones, or with one phone and a lot of app switching. Director Mode tries to solve exactly that. According to the developer, filmmaker Claudio Ripalti and his crew built it out of practical needs on documentary and narrative sets, and more than 250 filmmakers took part in the beta program before version 1.0 went live on the Apple App Store last week.

One app for Canon and Sony

The app is not affiliated with or endorsed by Canon or Sony, so it works through the remote interfaces that the camera manufacturers already offer. Canon Cinema EOS cameras connect through Canon’s XC protocol over Wi-Fi or LAN, Canon EOS R cameras through the Canon Camera Control API (CCAPI) over Wi-Fi or USB-C, and Sony Alpha and FX cameras over Wi-Fi or USB-C. The developer’s compatibility page counts 26 camera models. Some of them need extra hardware: the Canon EOS C70, C300 Mark III and C500 Mark II require an external Wi-Fi adapter, and LAN on the Canon EOS C50 needs a USB-C to Ethernet adapter plus Canon’s DR-E6P DC coupler.

The supported Canon cameras are the EOS C50, C70, C80, C300 Mark III, C400 and C500 Mark II on the Cinema EOS side, plus the EOS R1, R5 Mark II, R6 Mark III, R6 Mark II, R6V, R8, R8 Mark II, R50 V and the PowerShot V1. On the Sony side, the list covers the FX2, FX3 / FX3A, FX30 and FX5, as well as the a1, a1 II, a9 III, a7S III, a7R VI, a7 V and a7C II. One note here: the camera list in the App Store description is shorter than the one in the developer’s own feature chart (dated November 5), so I would check the compatibility page for your exact body before you buy anything.

What you can control depends on the camera, and the developer is open about it. On the Canon EOS R6 Mark III, the app gives you exposure, white balance, REC start/stop, tap to focus and tap to track, plus 6x magnification. On the Sony a7 V, you also get AF mode, half-press and one-shot AF, recording frame rate, S&Q settings and an app-based shutter angle mode, which keeps your chosen shutter angle when you change the frame rate. The Cinema EOS cameras add AF hold and the most complete telemetry, including battery, remaining recording time, color gamma and memory card status.

Director mode: four cameras on one screen

The feature that gives the app its name is the multicamera view. With Pro, you can monitor up to four simultaneous feeds in two-, three- or four-camera layouts, see the recording status of each angle, open the individual camera controls, and start or stop recording on all connected cameras with REC ALL. Tap to focus and tap to track also work inside the multicamera grid. On an iPad, that becomes a small video village for a solo operator or a two-person crew.

Besides the multicamera view, the app has a camera browser, a vertical control console that keeps the live view and touch focus on screen while you change settings, and a full-screen landscape monitor. For multicamera work over Wi-Fi, the developer recommends a dedicated 5 GHz access point, and it states that a Wi-Fi 6 access point with a real throughput of 300 to 400 Mbps can handle four cameras. A mixed setup is also possible: one Sony camera on USB-C plus up to three more cameras on Wi-Fi.

Monitoring tools and latency

The Pro monitoring tools are a waveform monitor, focus peaking, custom .cube LUTs, Canon Log monitoring LUTs, markers and frame guides, picture overlay and anamorphic desqueeze. That is a decent toolkit for judging exposure on a phone, and it is more than many manufacturer apps offer. Of course, an iPhone is not a calibrated reference monitor, but for checking framing, focus and exposure on a B or C camera across the room, it can be enough.

The developer has also published its own latency measurements. With USB-C, it measured about 30 ms from a Canon EOS R6 Mark III and about 40 ms from a Sony a7 V. Over Wi-Fi, the figures rise to about 110 ms for the R6 Mark III, 120 ms for the EOS C50 and 130 ms for the a7 V. These numbers come from the developer’s specific camera, device and connection setups, and I haven’t been able to verify them yet, but they suggest that the wired connection is the one to use when you pull focus from the app.

Basic or Pro: what you get for free

Director Mode Basic is free and supports one compatible camera at a time over Wi-Fi, LAN on Cinema EOS models, and USB-C on Sony cameras. Pro adds the multicamera console with up to four feeds, all the monitoring tools listed above, and USB-C for the Canon EOS R cameras. Focus peaking also requires Pro. USB-C connections need an iPhone or iPad with a USB-C port, the app requires iOS 17.6 or later, and the interface is in English only. There is no Android version.

Where does this fit? Canon announced its own Camera Control Centre software just a few days ago. It merges four of Canon’s existing tools, can compare up to four camera feeds, and will be a free download from January 2027, but it runs on a computer and is aimed mainly at Canon’s PTZ and remote camera systems. Sony, on the other hand, recently introduced the DP7 and DP5 camera control monitors for its Cinema Line bodies. FUJIFILM’s ETERNA ProRemote app, which we looked at during IBC 2026, also puts four cameras on one iPad, but only GFX ETERNA 55 bodies. My feeling is that a third-party app is the only realistic way to get Canon and Sony on one screen for now (I would love to see the camera manufacturers talk to each other a bit more, but I am not holding my breath).

Price and availability

Director Mode is available now on the App Store for iPhone and iPad. Basic is free. Pro costs $29.99 in the US and €29.99 in the euro App Store as a one-time purchase with lifetime access to all features. The developer calls this a special launch price, so I would expect it to go up at some point. More information, connection guides and the full compatibility list are on the Director Mode website.

Do you mix Canon and Sony cameras on your shoots, and how do you monitor them today? Would an iPhone or iPad replace a dedicated monitor for your B camera? Let me know what you think in the comments below!

entry.title: XTRA Muse 2 and Muse 2 Pro Global Launch Set for November 10 – 1-Inch Sensor, Dual-Camera Pro, 10-Bit X-Log 3
entry.summary: XTRA has announced a global launch on November 10, 2026, of two pocket gimbal cameras: the single-camera Muse 2 and the dual-camera Muse 2 Pro. The Muse 2 has a 1-inch sensor, 10-bit X-Log 2, 4K at up to 240fps, and 107GB of internal storage. The Muse 2 Pro pairs a 1-inch 20mm f/
entry.content:
XTRA has announced a global launch on November 10, 2026, of two pocket gimbal cameras: the single-camera Muse 2 and the dual-camera Muse 2 Pro. The Muse 2 has a 1-inch sensor, 10-bit X-Log 2, 4K at up to 240fps, and 107GB of internal storage. The Muse 2 Pro pairs a 1-inch 20mm f/2.0 camera with a 1/1.28-inch 60mm f/1.8 camera, records 10-bit X-Log 3, and shoots 4K at up to 240fps. However, XTRA does not say whether “global” includes the US, where the FCC is investigating the company.

XTRA announced the date in a teaser graphic that read, “New XTRA choices are here.” XTRA first previewed both cameras in April, when the company said on its blog that the Muse 2 and Muse 2 Pro were coming to the US. In July, we reported that XTRA had paused the US pre-orders for the Muse 2 Pro and refunded all deposits.

Two models, one form factor

In the teaser, both cameras have the same basic layout: a 3-axis gimbal on top of a handle, a swivel touchscreen, Zoom and Fn buttons, a joystick, and a record button. The Muse 2 has one camera in its gimbal head. The Muse 2 Pro has a taller head with two cameras, one above the other, and a larger body. This is the same split that DJI uses for the Osmo Pocket 4 and the two-camera Osmo Pocket 4P.

Muse 2: what changes from the first Muse

XTRA has not yet published a product page for the standard Muse 2, but a “Compare the Muse series” chart from the company lists its key specifications next to the first-generation Muse and the Muse 2 Pro. The Muse 2 keeps a 1-inch CMOS sensor on a gimbal and adds a 2x zoom that XTRA calls “lossless.” XTRA rates its dynamic range at 14 stops, up from 12.8 stops on the first Muse, and the color profile moves from 10-bit X-Log to 10-bit X-Log 2. Slow motion doubles from 4K at 120fps to 4K at 240fps.

The first Muse has no internal storage, and its touchscreen flips to one side only. The Muse 2 has 107GB of internal storage and a touchscreen that flips to both sides. Subject tracking moves from Smart Tracking with Focus Lock to an upgraded version of Master Follow, the tracking system of the Muse 2 Pro. A 1/4-inch thread is available on both single-camera models only through an add-on handle; the Muse 2 Pro has the thread built into an integrated grip.

The figures of the Muse 2 (1-inch sensor, 14 stops, 4K at 240fps, 107GB) are the same as those that DJI gives for the Osmo Pocket 4.

Muse 2 Pro: two cameras on one gimbal

For the Muse 2 Pro, XTRA’s store already has a full product page. The wide-angle camera uses a 1-inch CMOS sensor behind a 20mm-equivalent f/2.0 lens, and XTRA says that LOFIC (lateral overflow integration capacitor) technology gives it up to 17 stops of dynamic range. The second camera has a 1/1.28-inch CMOS sensor and a 60mm-equivalent f/1.8 lens, with 14 stops according to XTRA. The two lenses give 1x and 3x optical framing, and supported video modes add up to 12x digital zoom (240mm-equivalent).

The camera records 10-bit X-Log 3 in MP4 (HEVC). Standard recording goes up to 4K at 60fps. In Slow Motion mode, the wide-angle camera records 4K at up to 240fps and the telephoto camera 4K at up to 200fps, and both record 1080p at up to 240fps. Vertical video goes up to 3K at 60fps (1728 x 3072). Stills reach approximately 37MP, with manual exposures of up to 4 seconds.

Tracking, storage and outputs

XTRA’s Master Follow tracking keeps people, vehicles, and other selected subjects in frame at up to 12x zoom in supported modes, and XTRA says it works best in well-lit scenes. With Subject First, users can register up to three subjects for tracking and autofocus priority. Gesture control starts tracking or recording. The 2-inch OLED touchscreen reaches 1,000 nits, and rotating it powers the camera on and switches between horizontal and vertical shooting.

The Muse 2 Pro has 103GB of built-in storage and a microSD slot for cards up to 1TB. The 1,545mAh battery charges to 80% in approximately 18 minutes with a 65W USB-C PD charger, according to XTRA. For live work, the camera outputs up to 4K at 60fps over DisplayPort to a compatible capture card, works as a UVC webcam at 1080p, and streams over Wi-Fi through the mobile app.

These figures are very close to those of the DJI Osmo Pocket 4P, which also combines a 20mm f/2.0 camera on a 1-inch LOFIC sensor with a 60mm f/1.8 camera on a 1/1.28-inch sensor, claims 17 stops, and has 103GB of internal storage. Neither XTRA nor DJI has confirmed a connection between the two companies.

What does “global” mean for the US?

Since DJI was added to the FCC Covered List in December 2025, new DJI cameras cannot get FCC equipment authorization, and DJI does not sell the Osmo Pocket 4 series in the US. XTRA’s April announcement aimed the Muse 2 series at that market. On July 10, the FCC Enforcement Bureau proposed a $25,000 penalty against Xtra Technology LLC because, according to the FCC, the company did not answer a Letter of Inquiry about “disguised covered equipment.” We covered this in our article on the FCC’s fines against alleged DJI front companies.

The Commission then proposed to prohibit the import and marketing of previously authorized equipment from nine companies, XTRA among them. We could not find a final FCC decision on that proposal at the time of writing. The Muse 2 Pro product page went live on XTRA’s US store on October 28, but it marks the camera as unavailable in the United States, and it ships to Canada only. The standard Muse 2 does not appear on the store yet. Until XTRA publishes the launch details, it is not clear which countries the November 10 launch covers.

Price and availability

On XTRA’s store, the Muse 2 Pro Standard Combo costs $699, with the camera, a USB-C PD cable, a wrist strap, and a carrying bag. The Creator Combo costs $869 and adds a fill light, a mini tripod, a wide-angle lens, an Xtra Voko wireless microphone transmitter with a windscreen, a magnetic back clip, a battery grip, and a larger bag. The store shows these USD prices but ships to Canada only. XTRA has not given a price for the Muse 2. In May, the company wrote that the series starts “in the $600 range.”

B&H and CVP do not list the Muse 2 or the Muse 2 Pro at the time of writing. B&H carries the first-generation XTRA Muse and already lists the Freewell variable ND filter for the Osmo Pocket 4P and Muse 2 Pro. More information is on the XTRA Muse 2 Pro product page. We will update this article when XTRA publishes the launch details on November 10.

Do you think that XTRA’s offering is actually DJI products under a different brand? Don’t hesitate to let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: DaVinci Resolve 21.2 Released – PROLED XDR Touch Support, Gen 6 Color Science LUTs, Up to 5x Faster Rendering on M5 Pro and M5 Max
entry.summary: Blackmagic Design has released DaVinci Resolve 21.2, and the headline item is support for Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR touch screen. The update also adds support for Blackmagic Generation 6 Color Science LUTs and film looks, and Blackmagic claims up to 5x faster render
entry.content:
Blackmagic Design has released DaVinci Resolve 21.2, and the headline item is support for Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR touch screen. The update also adds support for Blackmagic Generation 6 Color Science LUTs and film looks, and Blackmagic claims up to 5x faster rendering on M5 Pro and M5 Max machines. Editors get multicam clips in source timelines, a shortcut to restore the last active edit points and source timecode for extracted audio, and Studio users get new AI assistant functions.

DaVinci Resolve 21.2, DaVinci Resolve Studio 21.2 and Fusion Studio 21.2 are available now as free updates for macOS, Windows, Windows for Arm and Linux. Blackmagic published the release notes on November 4, 2026. In both editions, the update adds support for the Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, support for Blackmagic Gen 6 LUTs, multicam clips that open as source clips in source timelines, compound clip changes, EXIF metadata in PNG files and a long list of fixes for audio, AAF, OGraf, H.265 and XDCAM media. The Studio version adds ResolveFX False Color support for Gen 5 and Gen 6 color science, new AI assistant functions and “multiple scripting API improvements”. System requirements do not change.

Version 21.2 follows 21.1.2 from late October, which made OGraf playback faster, refined edit point selection on the Edit page and added faster IntelliSearch analysis on M6 Macs in Studio. The larger feature release was DaVinci Resolve 21.1in September, with the native MCP server for AI assistants and individual HDR trims. For the full picture of version 21, read our coverage of the final Resolve 21 release and our hands-on with the Photo page and IntelliSearch at NAB 2026.

Touch and the M5 Pro and M5 Max

Apple announced the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display on October 28. It is the first Mac with a touch screen, and it uses a tandem OLED panel with 2000 nits peak HDR brightness. At the launch, Apple listed DaVinci Resolve among the third-party apps that would get Touch support later this year, but it did not say what the Resolve implementation would include. Resolve 21.2 now lists “Support for Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR touch screens.” The release notes do not say which pages or controls react to touch, or whether Resolve goes beyond the standard macOS behavior that translates touches into clicks.

The PROLED XDR models use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips that Apple introduced in March. In the download description for 21.2, Blackmagic claims “up to 5x faster rendering for M5 Pro and M5 Max Apple silicon chips”. Blackmagic does not say which render formats or which earlier version it compares against, so this is a manufacturer figure without a stated baseline. The item also does not appear in the readme itself, only in the summary on the support page.

Generation 6 color science

Both editions add support for Blackmagic Generation 6 Color Science LUTs and film looks. Blackmagic introduced Gen 6 color science to its software in September with Blackmagic RAW 6.0, and Resolve 21.2 now accepts the matching LUTs and film looks. In Studio, the ResolveFX False Color tool now also supports Gen 5 and Gen 6 color science, so exposure checks with false color work with the current Blackmagic camera color pipelines.

Editing: multicam, edit points and compound clips

Most of the editorial changes affect source timelines and edit points. Multicam clips now open as source clips in source timelines, and “Open in Timeline with Source Viewer” now supports both clips and multicams. A new menu action and keyboard shortcut restores the last active edit points, and a Command or Ctrl marquee selection now uses the last edit point type. This continues the trim and edit point work of 21.1, 21.1.1 and 21.1.2.

Compound clips get two changes. When you convert an in-out range to a compound clip, Resolve now replaces the clips in place in the timeline. A separate context action creates a compound clip from the in-out range without that replacement. The update also lets you conform lock multiple timeline clips to one media pool clip in one step.

Several smaller changes remove friction in daily work. The “stop playback” option now also applies to playhead nudges and mouse clicks, Edit menu options stay in place after a UI layout reset, and PNG files now carry their EXIF metadata into Resolve.

Audio and interchange fixes

For sound editors, extracted audio files now keep the source timecode. Blackmagic has also improved the decoding speed of MXF audio from network storage, fixed slow renders of MP3 audio-only files and corrected the channel order of WAV files with iXML tracks. An audio input device preference no longer resets after a restart, and pasted clip EQ Q and frequency values are now correct.

On the interchange side, 21.2 fixes missing clips in some AAF imports and wrong audio timecode in AAF files with interlaced media. Imported TTML subtitles now show italics correctly. For collaboration projects, source track changes in source timelines now work as intended.

AI assistants and scripting in Studio

The native MCP server that arrived in Resolve Studio 21.1 lets AI assistants such as Claude control a project with normal language. In 21.2, Blackmagic lists “improved AI assistant color and Fusion capabilities”. AI assistants can now download the extras that some advanced features need, and they can export frames or order thumbnails as a grid. Blackmagic gives no further detail on these functions. Studio also gets “multiple scripting API improvements”, and the Fusion tool and scripting reference documents are updated in both editions.

Media, OGraf and render fixes

Blackmagic lists a long series of fixes that affect camera media and delivery. They address slow loading of media from XDCAM drives, flashing media offline frames with some H.265 clips, a crash when decoding some multi-channel DNG files, file size estimates for spanned RED clips and artifacts in Sony XAVC Long GOP MXF renders. On Windows, the update fixes HE-AAC decoding of some clips and a GPU memory error with some OpenFX. ACES 2.0 artifacts on Windows and Linux are also fixed.

OGraf templates now load from network and zipped paths, and Blackmagic has addressed render timeouts and memory use with OGraf files. Other fixes cover the data burn scaling for render resolutions, render in place handles for frame-based formats, a hang when editing MultiText keyframes during render cache, missing Text+ inspector controls in older projects, an anchoring issue with Text+ CLS box extend controls, CustomTool LUT name controls, and network paths with accented characters on macOS 27. Studio users also get fixes for OpenFX that disappeared from MultiMaster trim groups on reload and for a render crash with MainConcept H.265 CRF encoding.

The standalone Fusion Studio 21.2 has its own list. The OGraf inspector now shows up to 35 template properties, and the update fixes OGraf loading and render issues, a material viewer crash with software rendering, the Shake random seed, script issues with the AddTool and SetInput functions, and the reading of video files with FFmpeg.

Before you install

The project library warning from the earlier 21.x releases still applies. Libraries stay compatible with DaVinci Resolve 20.3.2, but any project you create or open in 21.2 no longer opens in 20.3.2. Blackmagic recommends a full library backup and individual project backups before you update.

System requirements are the same as in 21.1: macOS 15 Sequoia or later on Apple silicon, Windows 10 Creators Update, Windows 11 for Arm on Snapdragon X Elite or NVIDIA RTX Spark, and Rocky Linux 8.6. NVIDIA users need Studio driver 581.57 or newer on Windows, 616.0 or newer on RTX Spark and 580.119.02 or newer on Linux. Monitoring through Blackmagic video hardware needs Desktop Video 12.9 or later.

Price and availability

DaVinci Resolve 21.2, DaVinci Resolve Studio 21.2 and Fusion Studio 21.2 are free downloads from the Blackmagic Design support center. The full release notes are available for the free version and for DaVinci Resolve Studio. DaVinci Resolve Studio is a one-time license at $295, which Blackmagic currently sells for $239 until November 20, 2026. More information is on the DaVinci Resolve product page.
